posts.title: Building Scalable Real-Time Applications with WebSockets
posts.excerpt: Learn how to architect real-time features that can handle thousands of concurrent connections without breaking a sweat.
posts.content:
Real-time features are no longer a luxury—they're an expectation. Users want instant updates, live collaboration, and seamless synchronization across devices. But building real-time applications that scale is challenging.

In this article, I'll share lessons learned from building CollabSpace, a real-time collaboration platform serving 10,000+ concurrent users.

## The Challenge

When we started, our WebSocket server could barely handle 100 concurrent connections before performance degraded. We needed to scale 100x while maintaining sub-100ms latency.

## The Solution

### 1. Horizontal Scaling with Redis Pub/Sub

We implemented a Redis pub/sub layer to enable communication between multiple WebSocket servers. This allowed us to scale horizontally by adding more servers.

### 2. Connection Pooling

We implemented intelligent connection pooling to reuse database connections and reduce overhead.

### 3. Message Batching

Instead of sending individual updates, we batch messages and send them every 50ms. This reduced network overhead by 80%.

### 4. Selective Broadcasting

We only broadcast updates to users who need them, using room-based subscriptions.

## Results

These optimizations allowed us to scale from 100 to 10,000+ concurrent connections while maintaining <100ms latency. Our server costs only increased by 3x despite 100x traffic growth.

## Key Takeaways

- Start with a solid architecture that can scale horizontally
- Use Redis for inter-server communication
- Batch messages to reduce network overhead
- Only send updates to users who need them
- Monitor performance metrics religiously

Building real-time applications is challenging, but with the right architecture, you can create experiences that delight users at scale.

posts.title: From Monolith to Microservices: Lessons Learned
posts.excerpt: Migrating from a monolith to microservices is challenging. Here's what worked (and what didn't) in our journey.
posts.content:
Last year, we migrated our monolithic application to microservices. It was one of the most challenging projects I've worked on, but it transformed how we ship software.

## Why We Migrated

Our monolith had grown to 200K+ lines of code. Deployments took 2 hours, and a bug in one feature could bring down the entire application.

## The Strategy

### 1. Start with the Strangler Pattern

We didn't rewrite everything at once. We gradually extracted services, starting with the least critical features.

### 2. Define Clear Boundaries

We used Domain-Driven Design to identify bounded contexts and service boundaries.

### 3. Invest in Infrastructure

We set up Docker, Kubernetes, and a service mesh before migrating any code.

### 4. Implement Observability

We added logging, metrics, and tracing to every service from day one.

## What Went Well

- Deployment frequency increased from 1/week to 10/day
- Team autonomy improved—teams could ship independently
- System resilience improved—failures were isolated

## What Didn't Go Well

- Initial complexity was overwhelming
- Debugging distributed systems was harder
- Network latency became a concern

## Key Lessons

1. Don't migrate unless you have a clear reason
2. Start small and iterate
3. Invest heavily in tooling and observability
4. Document everything—service boundaries, APIs, dependencies
5. Microservices aren't a silver bullet

## Conclusion

Microservices solved our scaling problems, but they introduced new complexity. The key is understanding the tradeoffs and having the right infrastructure in place.
